analysis.one_liner: Strikes the Affordable Care Act's premium subsidies, cost-sharing help, and the requirements to buy or provide insurance.
analysis.headline: A bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act's premium tax credits, cost-sharing subsidies, and individual and employer mandates was referred to three House committees in May 2013, never advanced out of subcommittee, and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The FREE Act would erase the part of the health law that helps people pay for insurance: the premium tax credits that lower monthly bills and the cost-sharing reductions that lower deductibles and copays for lower-income households [S2][S3]. It would also end the individual requirement to carry coverage (effective after 2013) and the employer requirement for larger companies to offer coverage or pay a penalty [S2][S3]. The bill's own findings describe the exchange subsidies as roughly $1.017 trillion in federal spending over eleven years, per a 2012 Congressional Budget Office report [S3]. Nothing in the bill replaces the help it removes.
analysis.who_benefits: Large employers (roughly 50 or more workers) would no longer face penalties for not offering coverage, and higher-income taxpayers would no longer help fund the subsidy program, cutting federal spending by roughly $1 trillion over eleven years per the bill's own findings [S3].

how_it_helps.text: It deletes Internal Revenue Code section 36B and ACA sections 1402 and 1412, ending premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions and the advance payments of both [S2][S3].

It adds a termination clause to the individual mandate so it stops applying to any month after December 31, 2013, and strikes section 4980H, the employer penalty, along with the related employer reporting requirement in section 6056 [S3].
It removes the employer-reporting paperwork under the Fair Labor Standards Act and makes conforming changes across the ACA, Medicaid, and tax code so the subsidy machinery disappears [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Low- and middle-income households buying coverage through the exchanges would lose the credits that reduce their premiums and the cost-sharing reductions that cap their out-of-pocket costs, and people with health problems would face higher premiums as the mandate's end pulls healthier people out of the insurance pools.
analysis.who_pays_short: Exchange shoppers and people with health needs

drawbacks.text: Repealing the premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions would strip the main affordability help from exchange coverage; the credits and reductions were how the law made plans reachable for people above Medicaid levels, and the bill includes no replacement [S2][S3].

Ending the individual mandate while keeping guaranteed coverage rules would tend to draw healthier people out of the insurance pools, pushing up premiums for those who stay; ending the employer penalty likewise removes a lever that pushed large employers toward offering coverage [S3].

The bill's own findings acknowledge the repeal targets roughly $1.017 trillion in federal support for coverage over eleven years, which is spending that currently reaches subsidy-eligible households rather than administrative overhead [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings accrue to the Treasury and, through avoided penalties and the tax structure, to employers and higher-income taxpayers, while the costs land on a specific group of people: those who rely on credits and cost-sharing help to afford plans, plus sicker enrollees facing worse risk pools. Because the bill replaces nothing, the trade is straightforwardly a transfer of help away from lower-income coverage shoppers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees, then sent to their health subcommittees, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Matt Salmon introduced the bill on May 9, 2013, and it was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce, with jurisdiction split among them [S1][S5].

The only further actions in its history were subcommittee referrals: to the Health Subcommittee of Ways and Means on May 10, 2013, and to the Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee of Education and the Workforce on July 8, 2013 [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and it expired when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People who buy coverage through the exchanges are better off, because the credits and cost-sharing help that pay part of their premiums and cap their out-of-pocket costs survived; large employers and higher-income taxpayers did not get the penalty relief and spending cuts the bill offered, since it never moved.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Exchange shoppers who kept their subsidies

for.name: Matt Salmon
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited ten original cosponsors; the bill text lists Reps. LaMalfa, Huelskamp, Jones, Franks, Radel, Schweikert, Meadows, Yoho, Gosar, and Duncan as joining at introduction [S3].

for.name: 48 of 232 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 48 cosponsors were Republicans, and no Democrat signed on [S4].

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: First-referred committee; its Health Subcommittee took no action
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 9, 2013, and sent it to its Health Subcommittee the next day; the subcommittee never marked it up or reported it [S5].

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 9, 2013, and took no recorded action for the rest of the Congress [S5].

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on May 9, 2013, and sent it to its Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee on July 8, 2013; no further action followed [S5].

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 48 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill [S4].

industries.note: The bill strikes section 4980H and the section 6056 reporting rules, ending the per-employee penalties on large firms that do not offer qualifying coverage [S3]. Their gain comes from no longer being pushed to provide coverage their workers would otherwise get.

Repealing the premium tax credits removes a large stream of subsidized customers from exchange plans, but ending the individual mandate also releases insurers from enrolling a broad, healthier pool [S2][S3]. Insurers' interest here does not run cleanly with or against the public: the subsidies help their customers afford coverage while the mandate forces people to buy.

The bill eliminates the tax credit machinery and the employer mandate, which per the bill's own findings represent roughly $1.017 trillion in federal support over eleven years, relief that accrues to taxpayers who fund it rather than to the households receiving the help [S3].
